title: Lecture #21: Immutable Classes in Java
topics: Why the class must be final

questions.question: What does it mean for a class like `Student` to be immutable?
options: Its fields are declared `static`, so all objects share one fixed copy
Once an object is constructed, its state can never change; any "change" requires creating a new object
Its objects cannot be passed to other methods or stored in variables
Its reference variables cannot be reassigned to point to a different object
questions.explanation: An immutable object's state is fixed for its whole lifetime once the constructor finishes. Whether a variable holding it can be reassigned is a separate matter: `Student s1 = ...; s1 = other;` just moves the reference and does not change either object.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the rules for writing an immutable class given in the lecture?
options: Declare the class `final`
Make every field `private` and `final`
Make defensive copies of mutable objects in the constructor and getters
Provide setters, but validate their input before assigning
questions.explanation: The lecture's rules are: mark the class `final`, mark fields `private final`, provide no setters, and defensively copy mutable (non-primitive) fields in the constructor and getters. Any setter, even a validating one, changes state after construction, which defeats immutability.

questions.question: Your `Student` class is immutable (final class, `private final String name`, no setters). A teammate needs a student whose name is "Rohit" instead of "Aditya". What is the correct approach?
options: Create a new `Student` object with the new name, leaving the original unchanged
Add a `setName(String n)` method that assigns `this.name = n`
Remove `final` from the class so a subclass can override `getName()`
Use `s1.getName() = "Rohit";` to overwrite the value through the getter
questions.explanation: With immutable objects, a "modification" is done by building a new object with the desired values, just as `String` methods return new strings. A setter would not even compile against a `final` field, and removing `final` from the class breaks one of the immutability rules. You cannot assign to a method call result.

questions.question: This is the lecture's first `Student` (final class, `private final` fields, no setters). What does `main` print?
options: `IIT G` then `IIT G`
It does not compile, because `college` is a `final` field
`IIT G` then `IIT B`
`IIT B` then `IIT B`
questions.explanation: The constructor stores the caller's `College` reference and `getCollege()` returns that same reference, so `s1.getCollege().name = "IIT B"` changes the object inside `s1`. `final` only stops the field `college` from being pointed at another object; it does not freeze the `College` object's own fields. That is why the lecture calls this version "not purely immutable".

questions.question: Which marked line fails to compile?
options: Line A
Line B
Line C
Line D
questions.explanation: Line B tries to reassign the `final` field `age` outside the constructor, which is a compile error. Line A compiles even though `college` is `final`, because it changes a field of the `College` object, not the reference itself; this is exactly why mutable fields need defensive copies. Lines C and D only read fields.

questions.question: In the lecture's fixed version (`Demo2.java`), `getCollege()` returns `new College(this.college.name, this.college.address)`. When `main` runs `s1.getCollege().name = "IIT B";`, what is actually modified?
options: The `College` object stored inside `s1`, because `getCollege()` still returns a reference
Nothing; the assignment is a compile error because the getter returns a copy
The original `college` object that `main` passed into the constructor
A brand-new temporary `College` copy, which is then discarded; `s1`'s own college stays "IIT G"
questions.explanation: Every call to `getCollege()` builds a fresh `College` with the same values, so the assignment changes only that temporary copy, which nobody keeps. The `College` inside `s1` is never exposed, so the next `getCollege().name` still prints `IIT G`. The assignment compiles fine; it just has no lasting effect.
questions.source: code: Demo2.java; notes p2 (deep copy diagram)

questions.question: In code review you see an "immutable" `Student` whose constructor does `this.college = college;` but whose getter returns `new College(...)` copies. The caller keeps its own `College c` that it passed in. Is the class safe, and why?
options: Yes: since the getter copies, nobody can ever reach the internal `College`
Yes: `private final College college` already prevents the object from changing
No: the caller can still run `c.name = "IIT B"`, which changes the student's college because both share one object; the constructor must copy too
No: the getter should return `this.college` and the constructor should make the copy instead
questions.explanation: Defensive copying is needed in both places. Without a copy in the constructor, the caller's `c` and the student's field point to the same heap object, so changing `c` later changes the student. Copying only in the getter covers the leak through getters, not the one through the original argument, so moving the copy from one place to the other just swaps which leak exists.
questions.source: notes p1-p2 (defensive copy in constructor / getter)

questions.question: Here the constructor makes a defensive copy, but the getter does not. What is printed?
options: `IIT G` then `IIT B`
`IIT D` then `IIT B`
`IIT G` then `IIT G`
`IIT D` then `IIT D`
questions.explanation: Because the constructor copied `c`, changing `c.name` to "IIT D" does not affect `s1`, so the first line is `IIT G`. The getter, however, returns the internal reference, so `s1.getCollege().name = "IIT B"` modifies `s1`'s own `College`, and the second line is `IIT B`. Only copying in both places makes the class truly immutable.

questions.question: The lecture ends by linking immutable objects to threads and race conditions. Why can one immutable `Student` object be shared by many threads without synchronization?
options: Because the JVM automatically places a lock on every `final` class
Because immutable objects are copied into each thread's stack, so each thread has its own version
Because no thread can change its state after construction, there is no write that could race with a read
Because `private` fields cannot be accessed from more than one thread at a time
questions.explanation: A race condition needs at least one thread writing shared state while others read or write it. An immutable object has no writes after construction, so every thread always sees the same consistent values without locks. The JVM does not add locks to `final` classes, and objects live on the shared heap, not per-thread stacks.

questions.topic: Why the class must be final
questions.question: A `Student` class has `private final` fields and no setters, but is NOT declared `final`. Someone writes `class FakeStudent extends Student` that keeps its own mutable `alias` field, adds `setAlias(...)`, and overrides `getName()` to return `alias`. What does this break?
options: Nothing: the parent's `private final name` field still cannot change, so every `Student` reference is still safe
Code that receives a `Student` may get a `FakeStudent` whose `getName()` result changes over time, so "Student objects never change" no longer holds; declaring `Student` final prevents this
It fails to compile, because a subclass cannot override a getter of a class with `final` fields
Only serialization breaks; ordinary method calls on `Student` still behave immutably
questions.explanation: Through polymorphism, a variable of type `Student` can hold a subclass object whose overridden methods expose mutable state. Callers that rely on `Student` values never changing (for example as map keys or shared across threads) are then broken, even though the parent's own fields are untouched. Declaring the class `final` (the first rule in the notes) blocks such subclasses entirely.
questions.source: notes p1 (CompSciStudent extends Student, rule: mark class final)
